about: JWT Trust Lab answers two separate questions about a JSON Web Token: is its signature valid for a secret you supply, and would your API accept its claims right now? Most online decoders blur those into one green tick. Here they are independent results, because a token can carry a perfectly valid signature and still be expired, aimed at another audience or issued by someone you do not trust.

You paste a compact signed token (a JWS with three dot-separated parts, optionally prefixed with `Bearer `). The tool decodes the header and claims, lists findings against an acceptance policy you configure, draws a timeline of issued, active, simulated-now and expiry times, and can verify HS256, HS384 or HS512 signatures against a local secret.

It runs entirely in the page. The README states there is no network access, telemetry, storage or third-party dependency, and the secret field is labelled as not saved. Verification uses WebCrypto when it is available. Inside the opaque-origin sandbox it falls back to a built-in SHA-2 HMAC implementation, which compares signatures with a constant-time loop.

It is a diagnostic aid, not authentication middleware. It does not verify RSA or ECDSA signatures, fetch JWKS documents or decrypt tokens. For turning individual segments into text by hand, [Encoder / Decoder](/encoder-decoder/) handles Base64URL, and [JSON Tools](/json-tools/) will pretty-print the decoded payload.

features.title: Decode without trusting
features.body: Header and claims are decoded from Base64URL, parsed as UTF-8 JSON objects and shown as highlighted JSON. The status line reminds you that decoding is not authentication.

features.title: Explicit expected algorithm
features.body: Verification needs you to pick HS256, HS384 or HS512 first. If the token header names a different algorithm the tool reports an algorithm mismatch instead of trusting the header, which is the habit that defeats algorithm-confusion attacks.

features.title: Acceptance policy
features.body: Optionally enter an expected issuer and audience. The audience check accepts a string `aud` or an array that contains your value. Clock tolerance runs from 0 to 600 seconds and defaults to 30.

features.title: Time travel
features.body: A simulated clock offset of plus or minus 10,080 minutes (seven days) shifts the tool's idea of now. You can see whether a token will expire tomorrow, or why one fails on a server with a skewed clock.

features.title: Header risk warnings
features.body: Warnings fire for `jku` and `x5u` remote key URLs, an embedded `jwk`, and `crit` or `b64: false` extensions, all of which change how a verifier finds keys or reads the payload.

features.title: Safe demo token
features.body: Load safe demo builds and signs a fresh HS256 token with the fixed secret `demo-only-not-production` and a 15-minute lifetime, so you can try every control without handling a real credential.

reference.title: What the checks mean and how a JWT is validated

blocks.text: A compact JWS (RFC 7515) is `header.payload.signature`, each part Base64URL-encoded without padding. The signature covers the ASCII bytes of the first two parts joined by a dot. JWTs (RFC 7519) are JWS or JWE tokens whose payload is a JSON object of claims. A JWE has five parts and is encrypted, so the tool rejects it with a specific message instead of showing garbage.

Parsing is strict. Input over 32,768 characters is refused. Segments must use only the Base64URL alphabet and cannot have a length that leaves a single stray character. The header and payload must decode as UTF-8 and parse as JSON objects, not arrays or scalars.
Findings are graded fail, warn or pass. The decision line says the claim policy rejected the token if any finding is a fail. Warnings do not change that decision.

Severity
Condition

blocks.text: Dates must be NumericDate values: whole seconds since 1970. A millisecond timestamp such as 1760000000000 is a valid integer, so the tool will not flag it as malformed. It will show a date tens of thousands of years away on the timeline and the token will look unexpired. Check magnitude when a lifetime looks absurd.

items: Choose the algorithm your API expects, not the one in the token.
The tool rejects the run if the header `alg` differs from your choice.
A secret is required. An empty signature segment returns not verified.
The HMAC is computed over `header.payload` using the secret's UTF-8 bytes and compared with the decoded signature.

blocks.text: RFC 8725 (JWT Best Current Practices) recommends exactly this: the verifier decides the algorithm from configuration, never from attacker-controlled input. The `none` algorithm and HMAC-with-public-key confusion are the classic failures it prevents.

Changing the token, secret or algorithm cancels any verification still in flight, so a late WebCrypto result can never label a different token as verified. HMAC secrets should be at least as long as the hash output (32, 48 or 64 bytes) for the algorithm to deliver its full strength.

example.title: Find out why an API returns 401 for a token that verifies

blocks.text: Scenario: your service rejects a token that looks fine. Start with the safe demo to learn the layout, then repeat the steps with your own non-production token.

items: Press Load safe demo. The token, the secret `demo-only-not-production`, issuer `https://demo.example` and audience `trick-it-demo` are filled in and the token is inspected.
Read the decision line. It should say claim checks passed, with a timeline showing issued and active at the same instant and expiry 15 minutes later.
Press Verify signature with HS256 selected. The status becomes HMAC signature verified.
Set Simulated clock offset to 20. This pretends it is 20 minutes later, and the decision changes to rejected with an expired finding, even though the signature is still valid.
Change Expected audience to `billing-api`. An audience mismatch finding appears. Restore the offset to 0 and the mismatch is now the only failure.

blocks.text: What to take away: the signature stayed verified through steps 4 and 5 while the claim policy failed. A 401 on a validly signed token almost always comes from `exp`, `nbf`, `aud` or `iss`. Compare the server's clock with the timeline, then raise tolerance only as far as your server's configured leeway.

limits: Only HMAC (HS256, HS384, HS512) signatures can be verified. RS256, ES256, PS256 and EdDSA tokens can be decoded and their claims checked, but not authenticated.
No JWKS fetching, key rotation handling or `kid` lookup: the tool never performs network requests.
Encrypted five-part JWE tokens are rejected, and detached or unencoded payloads (`b64: false`) are not supported beyond a warning.
Do not paste production signing secrets into any web page. Use a throwaway secret or the demo, and verify production tokens with your server library.
Claim checks cover `exp`, `nbf`, `iat`, `iss` and `aud` only. Custom claims, scopes and `sub` are displayed, not evaluated.

faq.question: Is it safe to paste a real JWT here?
faq.answer: The tool does not transmit tokens or store them, but a live token is still a bearer credential. Prefer expired or non-production tokens, and never enter a production signing secret.

faq.question: Why does decoding not prove a token is genuine?
faq.answer: The header and payload are only encoded, not encrypted or signed in themselves. Anyone can write a token with any claims, so trust comes from verifying the signature with a key you control.

faq.question: Why must I choose the algorithm myself?
faq.answer: If a verifier believed the token's own `alg` header, an attacker could request `none` or switch algorithms. Fixing the expected algorithm in configuration, as RFC 8725 advises, closes that gap.

faq.question: What does clock tolerance do?
faq.answer: It widens the time checks by up to 600 seconds to absorb clock drift between servers. It is added to `exp` and applied to both `nbf` and `iat`. The default is 30 seconds.

faq.question: Why is a RS256 token not verified?
faq.answer: Asymmetric verification needs a public key or JWKS and the tool supports HMAC only. Decode and claim checks still work, and the algorithm shows as unsupported for verification.
